content: Ingrowing toenails, also referred to as 'unguis incarnatus' or 'onychocryptosis,' occur when a portion of the nail penetrates the adjacent skinfold, leading to pain and discomfort. Various treatment options, both surgical and non-surgical, are available for managing this condition, but there is no universally accepted first-line treatment. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of both surgical and non-surgical interventions in a clinical setting, focusing on symptom relief, prevention of nail edge regrowth, and recurrence of the ingrowing toenail. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated these interventions, with a minimum follow-up period of one month. The search for relevant studies was updated to January 2010 and included databases such as the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and WEB of SCIENCE. Ongoing trial registries and reference lists of articles were also reviewed. Two independent authors selected studies, assessed their methodological quality, and extracted data. Outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). This updated review included 24 studies with a total of 2,826 participants, of which seven studies were also part of the previous review. Five studies focused on non-surgical interventions, while 19 evaluated surgical interventions. The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed, but incomplete reporting made it unclear for several items. Due to the nature of the interventions, participants were not blinded to their treatment (e.g., surgery or wearing a toe brace). Outcome assessors were blinded in only nine of the 24 studies. None of the included studies directly addressed the primary outcomes of symptom relief or nail regrowth. However, 16 studies evaluated recurrence rates. Secondary outcomes, such as healing time, postoperative complications (e.g., infection and hemorrhage), pain during and after the procedure, and participant satisfaction, were inconsistently reported. Two studies did not address any secondary outcomes. Surgical interventions were found to be more effective than non-surgical treatments in preventing recurrence. Specifically, surgical methods outperformed non-surgical approaches like gutter treatment (or gutter removal) and orthonyxia (brace treatment). In four of the 12 studies comparing surgical interventions with and without chemical ablation (e.g., phenol application), a significant reduction in recurrence was observed with the addition of chemical ablation. However, the surgical techniques used in these comparisons were not identical, making it unclear whether the reduction in recurrence was solely due to the chemical ablation. One study compared partial nail avulsion with matrix excision to the same procedure combined with phenol application. This study, which included 117 participants, demonstrated that the addition of phenol significantly reduced recurrence rates (14% with phenol versus 41% without phenol; RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.69). Postoperative interventions, such as the use of antibiotics, manuka honey, povidone-iodine with paraffin, hydrogel with paraffin, or paraffin gauze, did not show any significant differences in infection rates, pain levels, or healing times. In conclusion, surgical interventions are more effective than non-surgical methods in preventing the recurrence of ingrowing toenails. The addition of phenol to surgical procedures appears to further reduce recurrence and regrowth, although more studies are needed to confirm these findings, particularly where the surgical techniques in both study arms are identical. Postoperative interventions do not appear to reduce the risk of infection, pain, or healing time.
